opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot, and honestly it was one of the earliest decisions we wrestled with as a founding team.

The way we think about it is that the bottleneck in drug discovery isn't really the number of programs in the world. There are thousands of very capable teams at pharma companies and biotechs who know their disease areas deeply, who understand the biology, the clinical path, the regulatory landscape. What they're missing is better tools for the molecular design part: being able to predict how molecules interact, to design binders against hard targets, and to do it faster and with a higher hit rate than the traditional wet-lab-heavy approach.

If we built our own pipeline, we'd be picking maybe a handful of targets and placing concentrated bets. Drug development is a ten-plus year process with huge clinical risk, and most of that risk has nothing to do with whether your AI model was good. You can design a beautiful molecule and still fail in phase two because the biology hypothesis was wrong. So you'd end up with a company whose fate is tied to a few binary outcomes rather than to how good the technology actually is.

By building the platform, our impact scales with the quality of the models. Every improvement we make can show up across hundreds of programs at once, in areas we'd never have the expertise to pursue ourselves. That's a much bigger lever on the number of medicines that actually reach patients, which is ultimately what we care about.

There's also a focus argument. Building frontier models for molecular structure and design is extremely hard. It needs a team that's obsessed with the science of the models, the data, the evaluation. Running clinical programs is a completely different muscle. Trying to do both well at the same time, especially as a young company, felt like a recipe for doing neither well.

And partnering closely gives us something really valuable back: feedback from real programs. When partners take our designs into the lab, we learn where the models are strong and where they break, and that loop makes the platform better for everyone. So for us, being the infrastructure layer wasn't a compromise. It felt like the highest-leverage way to change how drugs get made.

r001.rationale: The response says the platform can affect hundreds of programs, but does not identify a bet that AI models will underpin discovery of most future drugs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the focus needed to build models with the different work of running clinical programs, but does not explain that an internal pipeline would divert resources from model improvement into clinical trials.

r003.rationale: The response describes partner feedback improving the platform, but does not say partnership revenue funds further model improvement.

r004.rationale: It says a pipeline would involve a handful of targets and binary outcomes, but does not say success on those targets could conceal a model’s failure to generalize.

r005.rationale: The response says partners take designs into the lab and report where the models are strong or break, providing external performance feedback that improves the platform.

r006.rationale: It distinguishes model-building from running clinical programs, but does not compare partner-facing model performance demands with an internal pipeline’s ability to compensate through downstream chemistry work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot, and honestly it's one we debated pretty seriously at the beginning. The pull toward building your own pipeline is strong, because that's where the biggest single outcomes live. If you own a drug and it works, that's an enormous amount of value. But when we really thought about what we wanted to be good at, and what we thought the world actually needed, we kept coming back to the same answer.

The thing we believe is that the models are going to get dramatically better, and that the rate of improvement is the whole game. If you're a company with one pipeline, you get a handful of shots on goal, and each one takes years and hundreds of millions of dollars before you learn whether you were right. That's a terrible feedback loop for improving a model. What we wanted instead was to be the layer that touches as many programs as possible, across as many targets and modalities as possible, because that's how you learn fastest about where the models work and where they fall down. Every partner we work with is effectively running an experiment that teaches us something about the technology.

The other piece is that drug discovery is not a problem that any one company is going to solve by itself. Pharma has decades of expertise in things we will never be the best at, like clinical development, manufacturing, regulatory strategy, understanding the biology of a specific disease. We don't want to replace that. We want to make the earliest, hardest part, which is finding the molecule, much faster and much more reliable, and then let the people who are great at the rest do the rest. If we do that well, we end up contributing to far more medicines than we ever could on our own.

And frankly, there's a cultural reason too. We're a research-driven company. We wanted a structure where the core thing we obsess over every day is model quality, not portfolio management. Being infrastructure keeps us honest about that. The customers tell you very quickly whether the thing actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says model improvement is central and favors broad infrastructure, but does not state that AI models will underpin the discovery of most future drugs.

r002.rationale: It describes an internal pipeline as a slow, costly feedback loop, but does not say pipeline work would divert resources into clinical trials.

r003.rationale: Partners are described as providing learning opportunities; the response does not connect partnership revenue to funding further model improvement.

r004.rationale: The response favors exposure to many targets and modalities, but does not observe that success on a narrow set can hide a failure to generalize.

r005.rationale: It says each partner’s program teaches the company about model performance and that customers quickly reveal whether the technology works, communicating external scrutiny of performance.

r006.rationale: The response distinguishes Chai’s molecule-finding role from pharma’s downstream expertise, but does not say that downstream chemistry can compensate for model shortcomings in an internal pipeline.

astra-6.text:
We chose infrastructure because the opportunity we’re excited about is making drug discovery more programmable. Rather than applying that capability to a handful of programs ourselves, we want to put it in the hands of teams working across many different diseases.

Pharmaceutical companies bring deep expertise in disease biology, clinical development, and getting medicines to patients. We can focus on building the models that help them design molecules with the properties they need. Those are complementary strengths.

There’s also a focus argument. Building a great AI platform and building a drug development company are both substantial undertakings. We wanted to concentrate on the underlying technology and make it useful across the industry.

r001.rationale: The response says it wants to make drug discovery more programmable and serve many diseases, but does not say AI models will underpin most future drugs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts building a platform with building a drug development company, but does not say an internal pipeline would divert resources into clinical trials.

r003.rationale: It does not describe partnership revenue funding further model improvement.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss narrow target success concealing a model’s failure to generalize.

r005.rationale: It does not say pharmaceutical partners provide external scrutiny of model performance.

r006.rationale: It does not distinguish partner-facing model performance demands from downstream chemistry compensating for shortcomings in an internal pipeline.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the question was where we could have the most impact. If you build a drug pipeline, you’re making a relatively small number of bets, and you need to build an organization around taking those drugs through development. That’s a very different company from one focused on building the best models for molecular design.

The infrastructure approach lets us focus on that core technical problem and work with pharmaceutical companies that already have deep expertise in disease biology, clinical development, and getting medicines to patients. If we can help those teams design better molecules and explore ideas they couldn’t pursue before, the impact can extend across many drug programs rather than just our own.

r001.rationale: The response frames infrastructure as a way to focus on models and help many drug programs, but does not say AI models will underpin most future drug discovery.

r002.rationale: It says an internal pipeline requires an organization to take drugs through development, but does not explain that this diverts resources from model improvement into clinical trials.

r003.rationale: It mentions working with pharmaceutical companies, but not partnership revenue funding further model improvement.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss narrow target success concealing a model’s failure to generalize.

r005.rationale: It describes helping pharmaceutical teams, but not external scrutiny of model performance or how that scrutiny prevents self-deception.

r006.rationale: It does not compare the performance demands on partner-facing models with an internal pipeline’s ability to compensate through downstream chemistry work.
